name: Kamboja
note: Identified in two branches — Param Kamboja (trans-Hindukush, around Kapisi) and Cis-Hindukush Kamboja (around Rajapura) — one of the few Mahajanapadas outside the Indian subcontinent proper.

name: Gandhara
note: Taxila became a major centre of learning (an early university) and Gandhara art in the centuries after the Mahajanapada period.

name: Kuru
note: The Mahabharata's Kuru dynasty homeland — the epic's Kurukshetra war is traditionally set in this region.

name: Panchala
note: Split into North Panchala (capital Ahichhatra) and South Panchala (capital Kampilya) — a recurring "two capitals" exam detail.

name: Kosala
note: One of the most powerful Mahajanapadas; annexed Kasi before later being absorbed into Magadha under Ajatashatru.

name: Kasi
note: Initially among the most powerful Mahajanapadas before being annexed by Kosala.

name: Vajji (Vrijji)
note: A confederacy (of clans including the Licchavis) rather than a monarchy — cited as an early example of republican/gana-sangha government; conquered by Magadha's Ajatashatru.

name: Malla
note: Also a gana-sangha (republic); Kushinagar is where the Buddha attained mahaparinirvana (death).

name: Chedi
note: Suktimati's exact location is debated among historians — placed in the Bundelkhand region between the Yamuna and Narmada.

name: Vatsa
note: Ruled by King Udayana; Kaushambi became a major trade and political centre after Hastinapur was reportedly flooded by the Ganga.

name: Matsya
note: Corresponds roughly to the modern Jaipur–Alwar–Bharatpur region of Rajasthan.

name: Surasena
note: Ruled by the Yadavas; among the earliest Mahajanapadas to accept Buddhism, per tradition.

name: Avanti
note: A major rival power to Magadha under King Pradyota, before eventually being absorbed into the Magadhan empire.

name: Anga
note: Champa was a noted centre of trade, reachable by river from the Ganga; Anga was eventually annexed by Magadha under Bimbisara.

name: Magadha
note: The Mahajanapada that eventually absorbed most of the others (under Bimbisara, Ajatashatru) and became the core of the later Mauryan Empire.

name: Asmaka
note: The only Mahajanapada located south of the Vindhyas, on the Godavari — often cited in exams for exactly that reason.

name: Shortugai
note: An isolated Harappan trading outpost far to the north, on the Oxus — evidence of the IVC's long-distance trade network reaching Central Asia for lapis lazuli.

name: Manda
note: The northernmost known Harappan site, on the Chenab near Akhnoor.

name: Harappa
note: Gives the civilization its name; excavated 1921 by Daya Ram Sahni. Known for its granaries and the later "Cemetery H" culture layered above it.

name: Ropar (Rupnagar)
note: First Harappan site excavated in independent India (1953); notable for a burial of a dog alongside a human.

name: Bhagwanpura
note: Shows a rare stratigraphic overlap of Late Harappan pottery with Painted Grey Ware — evidence for continuity into the Vedic period rather than an abrupt end. Its whole significance (the PGW overlap) is specifically a Late Harappan phenomenon.

name: Alamgirpur
note: The easternmost known Harappan site, marking the civilization's furthest extent into the Gangetic plain.

name: Farmana
note: One of the largest excavated Harappan cemeteries, giving useful skeletal/DNA evidence on the IVC population.

name: Rakhigarhi
note: One of the largest Harappan sites by area — larger than Mohenjodaro by some estimates — and a key source for ancient-DNA studies of the IVC population.

name: Banawali
note: Unusual radial (not grid) street plan; also yielded evidence of an actual ploughed field, rare direct evidence of Harappan agriculture.

name: Kalibangan
note: Known for rows of "fire altars" (interpreted as ritual hearths) and, like Banawali, a preserved ploughed field.

name: Ganweriwala
note: One of the largest Harappan sites by area, in the Cholistan desert on the dried Ghaggar-Hakra course — still largely unexcavated.

name: Kot Diji
note: A fortified pre-Harappan ("Early Harappan"/Kot Diji culture) site that shows the urban planning tradition already forming before the Mature phase.

name: Mohenjo-daro
note: The best-known Harappan city — the Great Bath, a planned grid layout, and an advanced drainage system are the standard exam references for IVC urban planning.

name: Amri
note: Type-site for the pre-Harappan "Amri culture", showing a transition from a regional Chalcolithic culture into the Mature Harappan phase.

name: Chanhudaro
note: The only major Harappan site with no citadel mound; known for bead, seal and weight manufacturing workshops — an industrial/craft centre.

name: Balakot
note: A coastal craft-production centre, especially for shell bangles — also significant as an early port on the Makran coast.

name: Sutkagan Dor
note: The westernmost known Harappan site, near the modern Iran border — thought to have functioned as a coastal trading post/port.

name: Dholavira
note: Famous for sophisticated water-harvesting/storage engineering and a Harappan-script signboard — a UNESCO World Heritage Site (2021).

name: Surkotada
note: Yielded bone remains identified by some archaeologists as horse — cited (with debate) in the domesticated-horse-in-IVC discussion.

name: Desalpar
note: A smaller, lesser-excavated Harappan site in Kutch, part of the same coastal Gujarat cluster as Dholavira and Surkotada.

name: Lothal
note: Site of what's usually cited as the world's earliest known dockyard — evidence of maritime trade — plus a major bead-manufacturing industry.

name: Kuntasi
note: A coastal trading and manufacturing outlet in Saurashtra, linked into the same maritime trade network as Lothal.

name: Nageshwar
note: A specialised shell-working (bangle/ornament) production site near Dwarka.

name: Daimabad
note: The southernmost major Harappan site — famous for a hoard of bronze artefacts including a chariot, now among the best-known IVC bronzes. Also has a later Chalcolithic (Jorwe culture) occupation layer above the Harappan one. Its famous bronze hoard belongs to this later, post-urban-decline phase.

name: Barbaricum
period: Ancient / early historic (dates vary by site)
features: Mentioned in the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea
note: A major port at the mouth of the Indus in the early historic period, described in the 1st-century CE Greek trade manual the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea.

name: Khirasara
period: Ancient / early historic (dates vary by site)
note: A Harappan-era coastal settlement in Kutch, part of the same Gujarat trade-port cluster as Lothal and Dholavira.

name: Broach (Bharuch / Barygaza)
period: Ancient / early historic (dates vary by site)
features: Mentioned in the Periplus as Barygaza
note: One of the most important ports of ancient India — the Periplus's "Barygaza" — a major hub for Indo-Roman trade at the Narmada's mouth.

name: Sopara (Shurparaka)
period: Ancient / early historic (dates vary by site)
note: An ancient port and Buddhist centre near modern Nalasopara — one of the sites of an Ashokan Rock Edict.

name: Kalyani (Kalyan)
period: Ancient / early historic (dates vary by site)
note: A Konkan-coast port active through the ancient and early medieval periods, mentioned by several foreign travellers/traders.

name: Chauf (Chaul)
period: Ancient / early historic (dates vary by site)
note: A Konkan-coast trading port, later continuing in importance into the medieval period.

name: Ghantasala
period: Ancient / early historic (dates vary by site)
note: An east-coast Andhra port with Buddhist stupa remains, linked to the Krishna-delta trade network.

name: Gopakapattana
period: Ancient / early historic (dates vary by site)
note: Ancient Goa's principal port, referenced in early medieval and maritime trade records.

name: Honnavar
period: Ancient / early historic (dates vary by site)
note: A west-coast Karnataka port on the Arabian Sea spice/trade route.

name: Nelluru (Nellore)
period: Ancient / early historic (dates vary by site)
note: An east-coast Andhra port town, part of the string of coastal trading centres along the Coromandel Coast.

name: Udyavara
period: Ancient / early historic (dates vary by site)
note: A west-coast Karnataka port near modern Udupi, part of the Malabar/Karnataka spice-trade coastline.

name: Kadura
period: Ancient / early historic (dates vary by site)
note: A minor Andhra coast port in the same Krishna-Godavari delta trading cluster as Masulipatam and Motupalli.

name: Kozhikode (Calicut)
period: Ancient / early historic (dates vary by site)
note: A major Malabar Coast spice-trade port, at its peak under the Zamorins in the medieval period — the port Vasco da Gama first landed near in 1498.

name: Masulipatam (Machilipatnam)
period: Ancient / early historic (dates vary by site)
note: Identified with "Masalia" in the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea — a long-running Andhra Coast port for textile and trade.

name: Muziris
period: Ancient / early historic (dates vary by site)
note: The single most-cited ancient Indian port for Indo-Roman trade — a major pepper-export hub; modern excavations at Pattanam are widely identified with the site.

name: Motupalli
period: Ancient / early historic (dates vary by site)
note: An Andhra Coast port, later noted in Kakatiya-period (13th century) inscriptions guaranteeing fair trade for foreign merchants.

name: Nirppeyarru (Mahabalipuram)
period: Ancient / early historic (dates vary by site)
note: The Pallava dynasty's principal port, still recognisable today by its Shore Temple and rock-cut monuments.

name: Korkai
period: Ancient / early historic (dates vary by site)
note: The early capital and chief port of the Pandya kingdom, famed in classical accounts for its pearl fishery.

name: Marakkanam
period: Ancient / early historic (dates vary by site)
note: A Tamil Coromandel-coast port in the same trading cluster as Arikamedu.

name: Arikamedu
period: Ancient / early historic (dates vary by site)
note: A well-excavated Indo-Roman trading settlement near Puducherry — Roman amphorae and pottery finds are direct archaeological evidence of the Rome trade.

name: Tondi
period: Ancient / early historic (dates vary by site)
note: A Pandya-era port on the Palk Strait coast, part of the pearl-fishery trading region alongside Korkai.

name: Tuticorin (Thoothukudi)
period: Ancient / early historic (dates vary by site)
note: Another key Pandya-coast pearl-fishery port, near Korkai at the southern tip of the Coromandel Coast.

name: Puhar (Poompuhar)
period: Ancient / early historic (dates vary by site)
note: The early Chola dynasty's principal port at the Kaveri's mouth — setting of much of the Sangam-era epic Silappatikaram; parts are believed to have been lost to the sea.

name: Dasarna
period: Ancient / early historic (dates vary by site)
note: A lesser-documented Odisha Coast trading point in the same coastal network as Manikpatna and Kalingapatnam.

name: Kalingapatna (Kalingapatnam)
period: Ancient / early historic (dates vary by site)
note: A port associated with the ancient kingdom of Kalinga, on the border of today's Andhra Pradesh and Odisha.

name: Manikpatna
period: Ancient / early historic (dates vary by site)
note: A port on Chilika Lake — excavations here have turned up Chinese and Arab pottery, evidence of Odisha's maritime trade with Southeast Asia and beyond.

name: Tamralipti
period: Ancient / early historic (dates vary by site)
note: The most important port of ancient Bengal — visited and recorded by Chinese pilgrims Fa-Hien and Xuanzang, and a major embarkation point for Southeast Asia.

name: Chandraketugarh
period: Ancient / early historic (dates vary by site)
note: An ancient port-city site near Kolkata, noted for exceptionally fine terracotta art and figurines from the Sunga–Gupta periods.

name: Mehrgarh
features: One of earliest farming sites in South Asia
note: A Neolithic-into-Chalcolithic site near the Bolan Pass, predating the Indus Valley Civilization by millennia — often cited as an ancestral culture to the Harappan tradition. One of the world's earliest known farming sites — its later Chalcolithic-phase layers (already noted) came centuries after this initial Neolithic occupation.

name: Lal Qila
note: An Ochre Coloured Pottery (OCP) / Chalcolithic site in the western Gangetic plain.

name: Atranjikhera
note: A long-occupation site spanning OCP/Chalcolithic through Painted Grey Ware and into early historic levels — useful for tracing cultural continuity.

name: Ganeshwar–Jodhpura
note: Type-sites of the "Ganeshwar-Jodhpura culture" — an early copper-using Chalcolithic culture in the Khetri copper belt of Rajasthan, thought to have supplied copper to Harappan cities.

name: Saipai
note: An OCP/Chalcolithic site in the western Gangetic plain, part of the same cultural horizon as Atranjikhera and Lal Qila.

name: Narhan
note: A Chalcolithic-to-early-historic site in the eastern Gangetic plain near Gorakhpur.

name: Imlidih
note: A Neolithic-Chalcolithic site in the eastern UP/middle Ganga plain cluster, alongside Narhan and Chirand.

name: Chirand
note: A key Neolithic-Chalcolithic site on the Ganga, known for a distinctive bone-tool industry.

name: Bangarh
note: A long-occupation site in North Bengal spanning the Chalcolithic through early medieval periods.

name: Ahar (Ahar-Banas culture)
note: Type-site of the copper-using "Ahar-Banas culture" of southeastern Rajasthan, contemporary with the Mature Harappan phase.

name: Gilund
note: A major Ahar-Banas culture settlement, notable for large mud-brick structures interpreted as possible administrative buildings.

name: Balathal
note: An Ahar-Banas culture site near Udaipur with an unusually early fortification wall for a Chalcolithic settlement.

name: Koldihwa
note: Cited for some of the earliest claimed evidence of rice cultivation in India, though the very early dating is debated among archaeologists. The disputed early rice-cultivation evidence here is specifically from the Neolithic layers, predating the site's Chalcolithic occupation.

name: Senuar (Senuwar)
note: A Neolithic-Chalcolithic site in the middle Ganga plain, part of the same cultural cluster as Chirand. Occupied continuously from the Neolithic through the Chalcolithic.

name: Eran
note: A long-occupation Chalcolithic-to-Gupta-era site; later famous for early Gupta-period inscriptions and a boar (Varaha) sculpture.

name: Kayatha
note: Type-site of the "Kayatha culture", one of the regional Chalcolithic cultures of the Malwa plateau.

name: Navdatoli
note: One of the most extensively excavated Chalcolithic (Malwa culture) settlements, opposite Maheshwar on the Narmada.

name: Gungeria
note: Famous for one of the largest Chalcolithic metal hoards found in India — copper tools/weapons plus silver ornaments.

name: Pandu Rajar Dhibi
note: A key Chalcolithic site of Bengal, giving its name to a distinct regional Chalcolithic cultural phase.

name: Mahisdal
note: A Chalcolithic site in Birbhum district, part of the same eastern Indian cultural horizon as Pandu Rajar Dhibi.

name: Rangpur
features: Late Harappan → Chalcolithic transition; type pottery
note: A Mature Harappan site in Gujarat, also significant for showing the Late Harappan → regional Chalcolithic transition — gives its name to "Rangpur ware" pottery. Its Period II B/C layers are a type sequence for the Late Harappan phase in Gujarat.

name: Prabhas Patan
note: A coastal Gujarat site near Somnath with a Late Harappan/Chalcolithic occupation phase.

name: Jorwe
note: Type-site of the "Jorwe culture", the dominant Chalcolithic culture across much of Maharashtra (c. 1400–700 BCE).

name: Golbai Sasan
note: A Neolithic-Chalcolithic site near Bhubaneswar, showing the transition from Neolithic to Chalcolithic material culture in coastal Odisha.

name: Nevasa
note: A major Jorwe-culture excavation site; also yielded important Old Stone Age (Palaeolithic) evidence in lower levels.

name: Inamgaon
note: One of the most thoroughly excavated Jorwe-culture village sites, giving a detailed picture of Chalcolithic house plans, granaries and burials.

name: Piklihal
note: A South Indian Neolithic-Chalcolithic site known for ash mounds interpreted as the remains of repeatedly burnt cattle pens. The ash mounds (burnt cattle-pen deposits) are the type example of South Indian Neolithic pastoralist sites.

name: Sanganakallu
note: A South Indian Neolithic-Chalcolithic settlement and stone-tool workshop site near Bellary. Also known as Sanganakallu-Kupgal — a major South Indian Neolithic settlement, stone-axe workshop, and rock-art site.

name: Burzahom
note: A Neolithic-into-Megalithic Kashmir site — known for pit-dwellings, a large menhir, and the unusual practice of burying dogs alongside their owners. Also has a later megalithic-period presence (a large standing menhir), which is why this site was previously filed under Megalithic — the pit-dwellings and stone tools are its primary, better-known identity.

name: Jagti
note: A Kashmir-valley site in the same regional megalithic/Neolithic cultural horizon as Burzahom (exact site identity/coordinates less well-documented than Burzahom's).

name: Kakoria
note: A central Indian megalithic site — placement approximate; less documented in mainstream sources than the major South Indian megalithic sites.

name: Kotia
note: A central Indian megalithic site in the same regional cluster as Kakoria — placement approximate.

name: Banimilia–Banhera
note: Megalithic sites in the Odisha/central-India cluster — placement approximate; less documented than the major South Indian megalithic sites.

name: Nartiang
note: Home to the largest cluster of standing monoliths (menhirs and dolmens) in Meghalaya, raised by the Jaintia people — a living megalithic tradition, not just an archaeological one.

name: Kuntitoli
note: A central-eastern Indian megalithic site — placement approximate.

name: Junapani & Takalghat
note: Neighbouring megalithic burial sites near Nagpur, among the better-studied Vidarbha-region megalithic cemeteries.

name: Naikund
note: A Vidarbha megalithic site notable for excavated iron-smelting furnaces — direct evidence of Iron Age metallurgy.

name: Amravati (Maharashtra)
note: A Vidarbha-region megalithic site — not to be confused with Amaravati (ancient Dhanyakataka) in Andhra Pradesh.

name: Dhanora
note: A megalithic burial site in the Gadchiroli/Vidarbha region.

name: Sisupalgarh
note: A large fortified early-historic settlement near Bhubaneswar, with megalithic-period antecedents — often discussed alongside ancient Kalinga's urban history.

name: Maski
note: Famous for the Minor Rock Edict that confirmed "Devanampiya" as a title of Ashoka — the discovery that first firmly linked the Ashokan edicts to Ashoka by name; also a significant megalithic burial site.

name: Hire Benakal
note: One of the largest concentrations of megalithic dolmens in South India, near Hampi.

name: Chandravalli
note: A megalithic-to-early-historic site near Chitradurga with Satavahana and Roman-trade-linked finds in later layers.

name: Hallur
features: Earliest evidence of iron in peninsular India
note: Cited for some of the earliest evidence of iron use in peninsular India, at the Neolithic-Megalithic transition.

name: Nagarjunakonda
note: A major early-historic Buddhist centre under the Ikshvaku dynasty, built over an area with earlier megalithic remains; now largely submerged under the Nagarjuna Sagar reservoir.

name: Amaravati (Ancient Dhanyakataka)
note: Ancient Dhanyakataka — a Satavahana-era capital and site of the Amaravati Stupa, one of the great Buddhist monuments of India; not to be confused with Amravati in Maharashtra.

name: Paiyampalli
note: A Neolithic-Megalithic transition site in northern Tamil Nadu.

name: Veerapuram
note: A megalithic-to-early-historic settlement site in the Krishna basin of Andhra Pradesh.

name: Jadigenahalli
note: A megalithic burial site near Bengaluru.

name: Palavoy
note: A megalithic site in the Rayalaseema region of Andhra Pradesh.

name: Brahmagiri
note: The type-site for South Indian megalithic culture — Mortimer Wheeler's 1947 excavation here established the Neolithic-Chalcolithic-Megalithic sequence used across the region. Also has an Ashokan Minor Rock Edict.

name: Sanur
note: A megalithic burial site (urn/cist burials) in northern Tamil Nadu.

name: T. Narsipur
note: A long-occupation site at the Kaveri-Kapila confluence, with Neolithic through megalithic and early historic layers.

name: Pazhayannur (Porkulam)
note: A Kerala megalithic site known for distinctive "umbrella stone" (kudakallu) burial markers.

name: Sittanavasal
note: Better known today for its later Jain rock-cut cave and murals, Sittanavasal also has megalithic burial remains nearby.

name: Kodumanal
note: A Sangam-era craft and trade centre with megalithic burials, Tamil-Brahmi graffiti, and evidence of iron and semi-precious-stone bead industries.

name: Mangadu
note: A Kerala site with a dense concentration of megalithic monuments (dolmens, menhirs, urn burials), now protected as a monuments park.

name: Adichanallur
note: One of the most important South Indian megalithic urn-burial sites, on the Tamiraparani — extensively excavated since the late 19th century.

name: Mitathal
note: A Harappan site in the same Haryana cluster as Rakhigarhi and Banawali, with occupation layers spanning Early to Late Harappan phases.

name: Damb Sadaat
features: Type-site of the Damb Sadaat culture
note: Type-site of the "Damb Sadaat culture", a pre-Harappan/Early Harappan phase in the Quetta valley of Balochistan.

name: Siswal
note: Type-site of the "Sothi-Siswal culture", a widespread Early Harappan phase across Rajasthan, Haryana and Punjab, ancestral to several Mature Harappan sites in the same region (Rakhigarhi, Banawali, Kalibangan). Also gives its name to the "Late Siswal" Late Harappan phase in the same region.

name: Jhukar
note: Type-site of the "Jhukar culture", a Late Harappan phase in Sindh marking the post-urban decline of the Mature Harappan cities.

name: Swat Valley (Gandhara Grave Culture)
note: The Swat Valley's "Gandhara Grave Culture" — a Late Harappan-into-early-Iron-Age regional culture, distinct from and contemporary with the decline of the Indus cities further south.

name: Mansehra
note: Major Rock Edict of Ashoka.

name: Shahbazgarhi
note: Major Rock Edict of Ashoka. Inscribed in Kharosthi script, unlike most Major Rock Edicts (Brahmi) — a recurring exam detail alongside Mansehra.

name: Kandahar
note: Major Rock Edict of Ashoka. Uniquely bilingual — Greek and Aramaic — reflecting the Mauryan empire's northwestern reach into Hellenistic and Persian-influenced territory.

name: Kalsi
note: Major Rock Edict of Ashoka.

name: Girnar
note: Major Rock Edict of Ashoka.

name: Sopara
note: Major Rock Edict of Ashoka. Same site as the ancient port of Sopara (Shurparaka) — a Major Rock Edict fragment was found here.

name: Sannati
note: Major Rock Edict of Ashoka.

name: Dhauli (near Shishupalgarh)
note: Major Rock Edict of Ashoka. Labelled "Shishupalgarh" on some reference maps for the nearby fortified city; the edict itself is usually specifically identified as Dhauli, in ancient Kalinga.

name: Jaugada
note: Major Rock Edict of Ashoka.

name: Bahapur
note: Minor Rock Edict of Ashoka.

name: Bairat
note: Minor Rock Edict of Ashoka. Same site as Viratanagara, capital of the Matsya Mahajanapada — this edict is also known as the "Bhabru-Bairat" edict, addressed to the Buddhist Sangha.

name: Bhabru
note: Minor Rock Edict of Ashoka.

name: Gavimath
note: Minor Rock Edict of Ashoka.

name: Palkigundu
note: Minor Rock Edict of Ashoka. A twin site with Gavimath, very close by.

name: Jatinga Rameshwar
note: Minor Rock Edict of Ashoka.

name: Siddapur
note: Minor Rock Edict of Ashoka. Close to Brahmagiri, part of the same Chitradurga-region cluster of Minor Rock Edicts.

name: Udegolam
note: Minor Rock Edict of Ashoka.

name: Rajula Mandagiri
note: Minor Rock Edict of Ashoka.

name: Nittur
note: Minor Rock Edict of Ashoka.

name: Topra
note: Pillar Edict of Ashoka. This pillar was later moved to Delhi (Feroz Shah Kotla) by Sultan Firuz Shah Tughlaq in the 14th century.

name: Meerut
note: Pillar Edict of Ashoka. This pillar was also later moved to Delhi (the Delhi Ridge) by Firuz Shah Tughlaq.

name: Nigalisagar
note: Pillar Edict of Ashoka.

name: Rummindei (Lumbini)
note: Pillar Edict of Ashoka. Marks the Buddha's birthplace; the inscription records Ashoka's pilgrimage and tax exemption granted to the village.

name: Rampurwa
note: Pillar Edict of Ashoka.

name: Lauriya Nandangarh
note: Pillar Edict of Ashoka.

name: Lauriya Araraj
note: Pillar Edict of Ashoka.

name: Sarnath
note: Pillar Edict of Ashoka. Topped by the Lion Capital — now India's national emblem.

name: Gujarra
note: Pillar Edict of Ashoka. (Corrected from an earlier pillar-edict classification — Gujarra is a Minor Rock Edict site, no pillar was ever found here.)

name: Kaushambi
note: Pillar Edict of Ashoka. Same site as the Vatsa Mahajanapada's capital — this pillar was later moved to Allahabad Fort.

name: Ahraura
note: Pillar Edict of Ashoka. (Corrected from an earlier pillar-edict classification — Ahraura is a Minor Rock Edict site, no pillar was ever found here.)

name: Sahasram
note: Pillar Edict of Ashoka. (Corrected from an earlier pillar-edict classification — Sahasram/Sasaram is a Minor Rock Edict site, no pillar was ever found here.)

name: Sanchi
note: Pillar Edict of Ashoka. Better known for its Great Stupa; the Ashokan pillar here bears the Schism Edict, warning against splitting the Buddhist Sangha.

name: Taxila
note: Same site as the Gandhara Mahajanapada's capital, centuries earlier — under the Kushanas it became a major centre of Gandhara art and Buddhist learning.

name: Kanauj
note: Later became far more famous as Harshavardhana's 7th-century capital, and the object of the centuries-long "Kanauj Triangle" struggle between the Palas, Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas.

name: Shravasti
note: Same site as the Kosala Mahajanapada's capital — one of the Buddha's most frequent residences.

name: Mathura
period: c. 1st century BCE – 550 CE (Shaka, Kushana, then Gupta)
note: Same site as the Surasena Mahajanapada's capital — also a major Kushana-era political centre and a distinct school of ancient Indian sculpture (the Mathura school).

name: Vaishali
note: Same site as the Vajji confederacy's capital, centuries earlier.

name: Varanasi
note: Same site as the Kasi Mahajanapada's capital.

name: Pataliputra
note: The Mauryan and Gupta imperial capital — modern Patna.

name: Kaushambi
note: Same site as the Vatsa Mahajanapada's capital and the location of an Ashokan pillar — three different eras of significance at one spot.

name: Rajgir
note: Same site as the Magadha Mahajanapada's capital, Rajgriha.

name: Mahasthan (Mahasthangarh)
note: Yielded one of the earliest Brahmi inscriptions in Bengal (Mauryan-era), and remained an important urban centre into the Gupta period.

name: Vidisha
note: Near Sanchi; the Heliodorus Pillar (2nd century BCE, predating the Guptas) is close by, recording a Greek ambassador's conversion to Vaishnavism.

name: Chandraketugarh
note: Same site already covered as an ancient port — also an important Gupta-era urban and craft (terracotta) centre.

name: Ujjayini (Ujjain)
period: c. 1st century BCE – 4th century CE (Western Kshatrapas/Shakas)
note: Same site as the Avanti Mahajanapada's capital — under the Western Kshatrapas (Shakas) it was a major regional capital before Chandragupta II annexed it for the Gupta empire.

name: Bharukachchha (Bharuch)
period: c. 1st century BCE – 4th century CE (Western Kshatrapas/Shakas)
note: Same site as the port of Bharuch/Barygaza — a major Western Kshatrapa (Shaka) port and administrative centre.

name: Shishupalgarh
note: Same site already covered under Megalithic sites (Sisupalgarh) and the nearby Dhauli Ashokan edict — this map doesn't attach it to one of the labelled dynasties, likely reflecting Kalinga's own independent history in this period.

name: Sopara (Shurparaka)
note: Same site already covered as an ancient port and the findspot of a Major Rock Edict fragment — also an important Satavahana-era port.

name: Paithan (Pratishthana)
note: The Satavahana dynasty's capital, Pratishthana — a major inland trade hub on the Godavari, linked to Roman-trade ports on the coast.

name: Dhanyakataka
note: Same site already covered as Amaravati (Megalithic/early-historic) — also a major later Satavahana capital.

name: Kodumanal
note: Same site already covered under Megalithic sites — this reference map doesn't pin it to one specific Tamil dynasty, reflecting the contested, shifting borders between the three Sangam-age kingdoms in this region.

name: Puhar (Poompuhar)
note: Same site already covered as an ancient port — the early Chola dynasty's principal capital and port.

name: Rana Ghundai
note: A stratified pre-Harappan/Early Harappan site in the Loralai valley, Balochistan — gives its name to a distinct Early Harappan pottery sequence.

name: Sarai Khola
note: A Neolithic-into-Early-Harappan site near Taxila.

name: Mundigak
note: A major pre-Harappan/Early Harappan urban centre in Afghanistan, showing the same cultural horizon extended west of the Indus system.

name: Kulli
note: Type-site of the "Kulli culture", a distinctive Early Harappan regional culture of southern Balochistan.

name: Naal
note: Type-site of the "Nal culture", an Early Harappan regional culture neighbouring the Kulli culture.

name: Allahdino
note: A small but well-preserved Early-to-Mature Harappan site near Karachi, notable for a gold/silver jewellery hoard.

name: Gumla
note: An Early Harappan site in the Gomal valley, showing a long Neolithic-to-Harappan cultural sequence.

name: Bhirrana
note: One of the earliest known Harappan settlements — some excavators date its earliest levels well before the conventional Early Harappan start, making it a key (if debated) site in dating the civilization's origins.

name: Rojdi
note: A key site for the long "Sorath Harappan" (regional Saurashtra) sequence running through the Late Harappan period.

name: Bet Dwarka
note: A partly submerged coastal Late Harappan settlement near Dwarka, studied through marine archaeology.

name: Bhagatrav
note: A Mature Harappan coastal settlement near the Narmada's mouth, in the same Gujarat cluster as Lothal and Broach.

name: Gufkral
note: A Kashmir Neolithic site near Burzahom, with similar pit-dwelling evidence.

name: Kili Gul Mohammad
note: Type-site for the earliest Neolithic culture sequence in Balochistan, predating the Kulli/Nal/Kot Dijian cultures.

name: Anjira
note: A Neolithic site in the same Balochistan sequence as Kili Gul Mohammad.

name: Sohagaura
note: A Neolithic-occupation site in the middle Ganga plain — later far better known for the Mauryan-era Sohgaura copper-plate inscription found nearby.

name: Lahuradewa
note: One of the key sites for very early rice cultivation evidence in the middle Ganga plain, among the oldest Neolithic sequences in the region.

name: Chopani Mando
note: A Mesolithic-into-Neolithic site in the Belan valley, close to Koldihwa and Mahagara, with some of the earliest evidence of pottery in the region.

name: Mahagara
note: A Neolithic site in the Belan valley, notable for cattle-pen post-hole evidence pointing to early animal domestication.

name: Kunjhun
note: A Neolithic site in the same Belan-valley cluster as Koldihwa, Chopani Mando and Mahagara.

name: Sarutaru
note: A Neolithic site near Guwahati, part of the distinct Northeast Indian Neolithic tradition (shouldered celts, cord-marked pottery).

name: Daojali Hading
note: A key Northeast Indian Neolithic site known for polished stone tools (shouldered celts) linked to Southeast Asian Neolithic traditions.

name: Napchik
note: A Northeast Indian Neolithic site, part of the same regional tradition as Daojali Hading.

name: Barudih
note: A Neolithic-Chalcolithic site in the Chota Nagpur plateau region.

name: Kuchai
note: A Neolithic site in Mayurbhanj district, part of the eastern Indian Neolithic-Chalcolithic cluster with Golbai Sasan and Mahisdal.

name: Erenda
note: A Neolithic site in the same eastern Indian cluster as Kuchai and Mahisdal.

name: Utnur (Utnoor)
note: One of the classic South Indian Neolithic ash-mound sites — burnt cattle-pen deposits, like Piklihal.

name: Tekkalakota
note: A South Indian Neolithic settlement site in the same Bellary-district cluster as Piklihal and Sanganakallu.

name: Budhihal
note: A South Indian Neolithic ash-mound and settlement site.

name: Watgal
note: A South Indian Neolithic settlement site, part of the same regional cluster as Piklihal, Sanganakallu and Tekkalakota.

name: Tilwara
note: A Mesolithic site in the Thar desert region of Rajasthan.

name: Bagor
note: The largest known microlithic (Mesolithic) site in India, with an exceptionally long, well-stratified occupation sequence.

name: Loteshwar
note: A Mesolithic-into-Chalcolithic site in North Gujarat.

name: Langhnaj
note: One of the earliest excavated Mesolithic sites in India, known for human skeletal remains alongside microliths.

name: Ratanpura
note: A Mesolithic site in the same North Gujarat cluster as Langhnaj and Loteshwar.

name: Damdama
note: A Ganga-plain Mesolithic site with a large excavated burial sample, part of the same cluster as Sarai Nahar Rai and Mahadaha.

name: Mahadaha
note: A Ganga-plain Mesolithic site known for multiple burials, including one interpreted as a double burial.

name: Sarai Nahar Rai
features: Early evidence of possible interpersonal violence
note: Famous for some of the earliest Indian evidence of human burials, including skeletons with embedded microliths suggestive of conflict.

name: Chopani Mando
note: Also covered under Neolithic sites for its early pottery evidence — its earliest layers are Mesolithic, making it a key site for the Mesolithic-to-Neolithic transition in the Belan valley.

name: Lekhahia
note: A rock-shelter site in the Vindhyas with notable Mesolithic rock paintings.

name: Baghor
note: "Baghor I" yielded a triangular stone on a platform, interpreted by some archaeologists as one of the earliest possible instances of goddess worship in South Asia.

name: Paisra
note: A Mesolithic open-air site in the Bihar plateau region.

name: Bhimbetka
note: A UNESCO World Heritage rock-shelter complex near Bhopal with an exceptionally long sequence of rock paintings spanning the Mesolithic through historical periods.

name: Adamgarh
note: A Mesolithic rock-shelter site near Hoshangabad, cited (with some debate) for early evidence of animal domestication.

name: Sundargarh
note: A Mesolithic site in the Odisha plateau region.

name: Dari-Dungri
note: A Mesolithic site in the same Odisha cluster as Sundargarh.

name: Gambharia
note: A Mesolithic site in eastern India, part of the same regional cluster as Kuchai and Birbhanpur.

name: Birbhanpur
note: A well-known Mesolithic microlith site on the Damodar, near Durgapur.

name: Kuchai
note: Also covered under Neolithic sites — Kuchai has both Mesolithic and later Neolithic occupation layers.

name: Sanganakallu
note: Also covered under Neolithic sites (as Sanganakallu-Kupgal) — the site has an earlier Mesolithic occupation layer beneath its better-known Neolithic settlement.

name: Renigunta
note: A Mesolithic site near Tirupati in southern Andhra Pradesh.

name: Tenmalai
note: A Mesolithic site in the Western Ghats region near Tenmala.

name: Teri Sites
note: A cluster of Mesolithic microlith sites on the red sand dunes ("teri") of the Tirunelveli coast in southern Tamil Nadu.

name: Sanghao Caves
note: A Middle Palaeolithic cave site in the Peshawar valley.

name: Pahalgam
note: Palaeolithic tools found in the Kashmir valley near Pahalgam.

name: Sohan Valley
features: Type region of the Soanian culture
note: Type region for the "Soanian" Lower Palaeolithic culture — among the first Palaeolithic industries identified in South Asia.

name: Pinjore (Haryana)
note: A Lower Palaeolithic (Soanian-related) site in the Siwalik foothills.

name: Anangpur
note: A Palaeolithic site near Faridabad in the Aravalli hills.

name: Buddha Pushkar
note: A Palaeolithic site near Pushkar in the Thar desert margin.

name: Didwana
note: A long Palaeolithic sequence site in the Thar desert, important for dating early human presence in arid Rajasthan.

name: Luni Valley
note: A Palaeolithic-bearing river valley in the Thar desert region.

name: Mogara Hills
note: A Palaeolithic site in the same Nagaur-district cluster as Didwana.

name: Bagor
note: Also covered under Mesolithic sites (as India's largest microlithic site) — has an underlying Palaeolithic presence in the same Banas-basin sequence.

name: Kalpi
note: A Palaeolithic site on the Yamuna in the Ganga-Yamuna doab.

name: Lekhahia (Belan Valley)
note: Also covered under Mesolithic sites for its rock art — the Belan valley sequence here extends back into the Palaeolithic.

name: Chopani Mando (Belan Valley)
note: Also covered under Mesolithic and Neolithic sites — one of the most complete Palaeolithic-through-Neolithic sequences known in India.

name: Paisra
note: Also covered under Mesolithic sites — has an Upper Palaeolithic open-air occupation layer, notable for possible hut-like structure evidence.

name: Las Bela (Balochistan)
note: A Palaeolithic-bearing region of coastal Balochistan.

name: Sabarmati Valley
note: A Palaeolithic-bearing river valley in Gujarat.

name: Baghor
note: Also covered under Mesolithic sites (for the possible early goddess-worship find) — the Son valley sequence here extends back into the Upper Palaeolithic.

name: Haora and Khowai river valley
note: Palaeolithic-bearing river valleys in Tripura, part of the less-studied Northeast Indian Palaeolithic record.

name: Sandhav
note: A Palaeolithic site in coastal Kutch, Gujarat.

name: Bhimbetka
note: Also covered under Mesolithic sites — its rock-shelter sequence begins in the Lower Palaeolithic, making it one of the longest continuously used sites in the world.

name: Adamgarh
note: Also covered under Mesolithic sites — has an underlying Palaeolithic occupation layer near Hoshangabad.

name: Baridih
note: A Palaeolithic-bearing site in the Chota Nagpur plateau (also recorded as "Barudih", covered under Neolithic sites).

name: Sundergarh (Odisha)
note: Also covered under Mesolithic sites — has an underlying Palaeolithic presence in the Odisha plateau region.

name: Hathnora
note: Findspot of the "Narmada Man" fossil (1982) — the first and so far only Homo erectus skull found in South Asia, a landmark in Indian Palaeolithic/human-evolution studies.

name: Rojdi
note: Also covered under Late Harappan sites — has an underlying Palaeolithic presence in the same Saurashtra sequence.

name: Sambalpur (Odisha)
note: A Palaeolithic-bearing region of western Odisha.

name: Hiren Valley
note: A Palaeolithic-bearing river valley near Gir, Gujarat.

name: Chalisgaon/Patne
note: Patne is a key Upper Palaeolithic site in Maharashtra, notable for some of the earliest ostrich-eggshell beads found in South Asia.

name: Dari Dungri
note: Also covered under Mesolithic sites (as Dari-Dungri) — has an underlying Palaeolithic presence.

name: Bankura
note: A Palaeolithic-bearing region of West Bengal, in the same broad cluster as Birbhanpur.

name: Nevasa
note: Also covered under Chalcolithic sites (Jorwe culture) — its lower levels are an important Lower/Middle Palaeolithic sequence.

name: Bori
features: Dated by a volcanic ash layer
note: One of the oldest dated Acheulian (Lower Palaeolithic) sites in India, its age fixed by a volcanic ash layer linked to the Toba super-eruption horizon.

name: Hunsgi
note: A major Lower Palaeolithic (Acheulian) site in the Hunsgi-Baichbal valley, notable for well-preserved evidence of tool-making "living floors".

name: Betamcharla
note: A Palaeolithic site in the Kurnool district cluster.

name: Malprabha
note: A Palaeolithic-bearing river valley in northern Karnataka.

name: Kurnool (caves)
note: The Kurnool caves preserve a long Upper Palaeolithic-into-Mesolithic occupation sequence, along with rich faunal remains.

name: Koloshi Cave
note: A Palaeolithic cave site in the Mandovi valley region of Goa.

name: Lingsugur
note: A Palaeolithic site in the same Raichur-district cluster as Hunsgi.

name: Mandovi Valley
note: A Palaeolithic-bearing river valley in Goa.

name: Chittoor
note: A Palaeolithic-bearing region of southern Andhra Pradesh.

name: Renigunta
note: Also covered under Mesolithic sites — has an underlying Palaeolithic presence near Tirupati.

name: Gudiyam Cave
note: A Palaeolithic cave site near Chennai.

name: Attirampakkam
features: Among the oldest dated Acheulian sites in South Asia
note: One of the most significant Palaeolithic sites in India — dating here pushed back the age of Acheulian (Lower Palaeolithic) tool-making in South Asia to over a million years.

name: Pallavaram
features: Robert Bruce Foote's first Indian Palaeolithic find, 1863
note: Where Robert Bruce Foote found the first recognised Palaeolithic (Acheulian) tool in India in 1863 — the discovery that opened Indian Palaeolithic archaeology as a field.

name: Odai
note: A Palaeolithic site in the same Chennai-region cluster as Attirampakkam and Pallavaram.

name: Palghat
note: A Palaeolithic-bearing site near the Palakkad Gap, the main lowland corridor through the Western Ghats.

name: Palakkad
note: Listed separately on the reference map alongside Palghat (an older transliteration of the same town) — kept as its own marker, nudged slightly so both remain visible, rather than assuming they're identical.

name: Teri Sites
note: Also covered under Mesolithic sites — the red sand-dune "teri" sites have an underlying Palaeolithic presence too.

name: Archaeological Site of Nalanda Mahavihara
note: Ruins of the great Nalanda Mahavihara, one of the world's oldest residential universities — a major centre of Buddhist learning under Gupta and later patronage.

name: Mahabodhi Temple Complex
period: 3rd century BCE onward (present temple mainly Gupta-era)
note: Marks the spot at Bodh Gaya where the Buddha is said to have attained enlightenment — one of the four most sacred Buddhist pilgrimage sites.

name: Khajuraho Group of Monuments
note: Chandela-era temples famous for elaborate sculptural work, including their well-known erotic friezes — a distinct Nagara-style architectural school.

name: Rani ki Vav
note: An elaborately sculpted stepwell built by the Solanki (Chalukya) dynasty — a distinctive form of ancient Indian water architecture.

name: Dholavira
note: Also covered under Harappan (Mature) sites — its water-engineering and urban planning are what earned it UNESCO recognition, alongside Mohenjodaro-level significance.

name: Champaner-Pavagadh Archaeological Park
note: An unusually complete pre-Mughal Islamic city, alongside earlier Hindu/Jain temple remains on Pavagadh hill — one of the few unrelocated historic capitals of its period.

name: Buddhist Monuments at Sanchi
note: Also covered under Important Kingdoms & Towns — India's oldest surviving stone Buddhist sanctuary, begun under Ashoka, with its famous carved gateways (toranas) added under the Satavahanas.

name: Rock Shelters of Bhimbetka
note: Also covered under Palaeolithic and Mesolithic sites — recognised by UNESCO for its exceptionally long rock-art sequence, one of the longest anywhere in the world.

name: Ellora Caves
note: A rock-cut cave complex uniquely combining Buddhist, Hindu and Jain monuments side by side, including the monolithic Kailasa Temple carved from a single rock.

name: Ajanta Caves
note: Rock-cut Buddhist caves famed for their surviving murals and paintings, mostly patronised under the Vakataka dynasty.

name: Elephanta Caves
note: Rock-cut Shiva temple caves on an island near Mumbai, notable for the Trimurti sculpture.

name: Sun Temple, Konark
note: Built under the Eastern Ganga dynasty in the form of a colossal stone chariot dedicated to the sun god Surya.

name: Kakatiya Rudreshwara (Ramappa) Temple
note: A Kakatiya-dynasty temple noted for its lightweight "floating bricks" and earthquake-resistant sandbox foundation technique.

name: Group of Monuments at Pattadakal
note: A Chalukya-dynasty temple complex showing a deliberate blend of Nagara (north Indian) and Dravida (south Indian) architectural styles side by side.

name: Group of Monuments at Hampi
note: Ruins of Vijayanagara, capital of the Vijayanagara Empire — one of the largest and best-preserved medieval city sites in India.

name: Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram
note: Also covered under Important Kingdoms & Towns as the Pallava dynasty's port — its rock-cut rathas and the Shore Temple are what earned the UNESCO listing specifically.

name: Great Living Chola Temples
note: A serial listing of three Chola-dynasty temples (Thanjavur, Gangaikonda Cholapuram, Darasuram) — Thanjavur's Brihadeeswarar Temple is the best known, built under Raja Raja Chola I.

name: Lakhudiyar
note: A rock-shelter site in the Kumaon hills with prehistoric rock paintings (animals, human figures, geometric patterns).

name: Bhimbetka Rock Shelter Caves and Painting
note: Also covered under Palaeolithic, Mesolithic and World Heritage sites — one of the world's longest continuous rock-art sequences.

name: Barabar Caves
features: Oldest surviving rock-cut caves in India
note: The oldest surviving rock-cut caves in India, gifted by Ashoka (and later Dasharatha Maurya) to the Ajivika sect — famous for their mirror-polished interior walls.

name: Udayagiri Caves
note: Gupta-era rock-cut caves near Vidisha, famous for a large relief panel of Vishnu's Varaha (boar) avatar rescuing the earth goddess.

name: Adamgarh Rock Shelter Caves and Painting
note: Also covered under Palaeolithic and Mesolithic sites — rock shelters near Hoshangabad with prehistoric paintings.

name: Jogimara Caves
note: Known for some of the earliest surviving cave paintings and inscriptions in India, alongside the nearby Sitabenga cave (an early rock-cut "theatre").

name: Bagh Caves
note: Buddhist rock-cut caves with murals in a style close to Ajanta's, though more damaged/faded today.

name: Ellora Caves
note: Also covered under World Heritage sites — Buddhist, Hindu and Jain caves side by side, including the monolithic Kailasa Temple.

name: Ajanta Caves
note: Also covered under World Heritage sites — Buddhist caves famed for their surviving murals.

name: Pandavleni Caves (Nasik Caves)
note: Buddhist caves near Nashik with important early inscriptions, including Satavahana-era donative records.

name: Udayagiri-Khandagiri Caves
note: Jain rock-cut caves near Bhubaneswar; the Hathigumpha inscription here, by King Kharavela of Kalinga, is a major source for early Kalinga history.

name: Kanheri Caves
note: A large Buddhist cave complex in present-day Mumbai (Sanjay Gandhi National Park), with over a hundred caves.

name: Elephanta Caves
note: Also covered under World Heritage sites — rock-cut Shiva caves on an island near Mumbai, notable for the Trimurti sculpture.

name: Karla Caves
features: Largest chaitya hall of its kind in India
note: Home to the largest and best-preserved rock-cut Buddhist chaitya (prayer hall) in India, from the Satavahana period.

name: Bedse Caves
note: Buddhist rock-cut caves near Karla, in the same Pune-district cluster as the Bhaja caves.

name: Guntupalli Caves
note: A Buddhist rock-cut monastic complex in coastal Andhra, with a notable circular chaitya hall.

name: Badami Caves
note: Chalukya-dynasty rock-cut temples (Hindu and Jain) carved into a sandstone cliff — an early example of Deccan rock-cut architecture.

name: Undavalli Caves
note: Rock-cut cave temples near Vijayawada, with a notable multi-tiered structure and a large reclining Vishnu sculpture.

name: Mahabalipuram Caves
note: Also covered under World Heritage sites and Important Kingdoms & Towns — Pallava-era rock-cut cave temples alongside the more famous open-air rathas and Shore Temple.

name: Edakkal Rock Shelter Caves and Painting
note: A Wayanad rock shelter famous for petroglyphs (rock carvings), among the earliest evidence of a script-like system in South India.

name: Sittanavasal Caves
note: Also covered under Megalithic sites — better known today for its Jain rock-cut cave and murals.

name: Yerragudi
note: Major Rock Edict of Ashoka; unusually, Yerragudi also has Minor Rock Edicts inscribed at the same site, making it one of the few places with both.

name: Sankissa (Sankisya)
note: An Ashokan pillar (elephant capital) at Sankissa — traditionally one of the sites the Buddha is said to have visited; the pillar itself carries no lengthy inscribed edict text.

name: Nilgirva
note: Listed separately on the reference map close to Nigali Sagar — likely the same or an adjoining Nepal Tarai pillar site under a variant name; kept as its own marker, nudged slightly, to match the source rather than assuming they're identical.

name: Rupandehi
note: The Nepal district containing Rummindei (Lumbini) and Nigali Sagar — shown as its own marker on the reference map, likely marking the district/region rather than a distinct third pillar.

name: Allahabad Pillar
note: The Kaushambi pillar, physically moved to Allahabad Fort — later also inscribed with Samudragupta's Gupta-era Prayaga Prashasti, making it a rare monument bearing both Mauryan and Gupta inscriptions.

name: Hastinapur
note: Also covered under Mahajanapadas (Kuru capital) — an important Jain pilgrimage town, associated with three Tirthankaras.

name: Mathura
note: Also covered under Mahajanapadas, Important Kingdoms & Towns — a major early centre of Jain art (the Kankali Tila mound yielded extensive Jain sculpture).

name: Shravasti
note: Also covered under Mahajanapadas — associated with Sambhavanatha, the third Tirthankara.

name: Saketa (Ayodhya)
note: Traditionally associated with five Tirthankaras, including the first, Rishabhanatha.

name: Varanasi (Banaras/Kasi)
note: Also covered under Mahajanapadas — associated with Parshvanatha (23rd Tirthankara) and Suparshvanatha.

name: Vaishali
note: Also covered under Mahajanapadas — traditionally cited as Mahavira's birthplace (alongside nearby Kundalpur/Kundagrama).

name: Sarnath
note: Also covered under Ashokan Pillar Edicts — better known as a Buddhist site, but also has Jain associations and remains.

name: Pataliputra
note: Also covered under Important Kingdoms & Towns — site of an early Jain council under the Mauryas, per Jain tradition.

name: Rajgir (Rajagriha)
note: Also covered under Mahajanapadas, Important Kingdoms & Towns — a major early centre for both Jainism and Buddhism.

name: Parasnath (Shikharji)
note: Considered the most sacred Jain pilgrimage site — twenty of the twenty-four Tirthankaras are believed to have attained moksha (liberation) here.

name: Mount Abu
note: Home to the Dilwara Temples, famed for exceptionally intricate marble carving (mainly medieval, 11th–13th century).

name: Deogarh
note: A major Jain temple complex (alongside Hindu temples) with a large concentration of Jain sculpture and inscriptions.

name: Udaigiri Caves
note: Also covered under Ancient Cave Sites — better known for its Gupta-era Varaha panel, but also has Jain cave shrines.

name: Kundalpur
note: Traditionally cited (alongside Vaishali) as Mahavira's birthplace, Kundagrama.

name: Pawapuri
note: Where Mahavira is believed to have attained nirvana (death) — one of the most important Jain pilgrimage sites.

name: Besnagar
note: An ancient town near Vidisha with Jain remains, close to the Heliodorus Pillar site.

name: Khajuraho
note: Also covered under World Heritage sites — best known for its Hindu temples, but also has a significant group of Jain temples in the same complex.

name: Vallabhi
note: Site of the Council of Valabhi (c. 5th–6th century CE), where the Jain canon (Agamas) was finally compiled and written down.

name: Girnar
note: Also covered under Ashokan Major Rock Edicts — Girnar hill is also a major Jain (and Hindu) pilgrimage site, associated with Neminatha, the 22nd Tirthankara.

name: Palitana (Shatrunjaya)
note: The Shatrunjaya hill above Palitana holds one of the largest concentrations of Jain temples anywhere — thousands of shrines built over centuries.

name: Sirpur
note: An early-historic archaeological site with Buddhist, Hindu and Jain remains side by side.

name: Udayagiri-Khandagiri Caves
note: Also covered under Ancient Cave Sites — Jain rock-cut caves near Bhubaneswar, with the Hathigumpha inscription of King Kharavela.

name: Ellora Caves
note: Also covered under World Heritage and Cave sites — includes a distinct group of Jain caves alongside its Buddhist and Hindu ones.

name: Pratishthana (Paithan)
note: Also covered under Important Kingdoms & Towns (Satavahana capital) — also had an early Jain presence.

name: Aihole
note: An early Chalukya-dynasty temple town with a notable Jain temple (Meguti) alongside its many Hindu temples.

name: Pattadakal
note: Also covered under World Heritage sites — mainly a Chalukya Hindu temple complex, with some Jain presence nearby.

name: Badami Caves
note: Also covered under Ancient Cave Sites — one of its four rock-cut caves is a dedicated Jain cave temple.

name: Shravanabelagola
note: Home to the monolithic Gomateshwara (Bahubali) statue — one of the tallest monolithic statues in the world and among the most important Jain pilgrimage sites in South India.

name: Kanchipuram
note: An early centre of Jainism in Tamil Nadu alongside its later fame as a temple city under the Pallavas and Cholas.

name: Sittanavasal Caves
note: Also covered under Megalithic and Cave sites — a Jain rock-cut cave with notable frescoes, among the finest surviving early Jain paintings in India.

name: Lumbini
note: Also covered under Ashokan Pillar Edicts (as Rummindei) — the Buddha's birthplace, marked by an Ashokan pillar recording his pilgrimage there.

name: Shravasti
note: Also covered under Mahajanapadas and Jain sites — one of the Buddha's most frequent residences, site of the Jetavana monastery.

name: Kusinagara (Kushinagar)
note: Also covered under Mahajanapadas (Malla capital) — where the Buddha attained mahaparinirvana (death).

name: Sarnath
features: Site of the Buddha's first sermon
note: Also covered under Ashokan Pillar Edicts and Jain sites — where the Buddha delivered his first sermon; the Ashokan Lion Capital here is India's national emblem.

name: Barabar
note: Also covered under Ancient Cave Sites — the oldest surviving rock-cut caves in India, gifted by Ashoka to the (non-Buddhist) Ajivika sect, though close to the core Buddhist heartland.

name: Bodh Gaya
note: Also covered under World Heritage sites (Mahabodhi Temple Complex) — where the Buddha attained enlightenment, the most sacred Buddhist pilgrimage site.

name: Bharhut
note: Site of a Shunga-era stupa famous for its carved railings and gateway — among the earliest and most detailed narrative Buddhist relief sculpture in India.

name: Sanchi
note: Also covered under World Heritage, Important Kingdoms & Towns, and Jain sites — India's oldest surviving stone Buddhist stupa complex, begun under Ashoka.

name: Nasik (Pandavleni Caves)
note: Also covered under Ancient Cave Sites — Buddhist caves with important early Satavahana-era donative inscriptions.

name: Ajanta
note: Also covered under World Heritage and Cave sites — Buddhist caves famed for their surviving murals, mostly Vakataka-era.

name: Junnar
note: A large Buddhist rock-cut cave complex near Pune, with over 200 caves across several hills.

name: Karle (Karla Caves)
note: Also covered under Ancient Cave Sites — home to the largest rock-cut Buddhist chaitya hall in India.

name: Nagarjunakonda
note: Also covered under Megalithic sites — a major Buddhist centre under the Ikshvaku dynasty, now largely submerged under the Nagarjuna Sagar reservoir.

name: Amaravati
note: Also covered under Megalithic and Important Kingdoms & Towns — site of the Amaravati Stupa, one of the great Buddhist monuments of India, and its own distinct school of Buddhist sculpture.

name: Bamyan
note: Site of two colossal rock-cut standing Buddha statues, once among the largest in the world, destroyed by the Taliban in 2001 — marks the extent of Buddhist influence into Central Asia.

name: Taxila
note: Also covered under Mahajanapadas, Important Kingdoms & Towns — a major centre of Buddhist learning and Gandhara art under the Kushanas.

name: Sanghol
note: A Kushana-era Buddhist site in Punjab, known for a notable stupa and railing sculptures.

name: Kapilvastu
note: The Buddha's hometown, where he spent his early life before renouncing it — its exact location (Tilaurakot in Nepal, or Piprahwa in UP) is still debated.

name: Kesariya
features: Tallest known stupa in the world
note: Home to what's usually cited as the tallest known stupa in the world, larger in base area than even Borobudur.

name: Vikramashila
note: One of the two most important Buddhist monastic universities of the Pala period, alongside Nalanda — founded by Dharmapala.

name: Sankissa
note: Also covered under Ashokan Pillar Edicts and Jain sites — traditionally where the Buddha is said to have descended back to earth after preaching to his mother in heaven.

name: Nalanda
note: Also covered under World Heritage sites — one of the world's oldest residential universities, a major centre of Buddhist learning under Gupta and Pala patronage.

name: Mahasthanagarh
note: Also covered under Neolithic and Important Kingdoms & Towns — an ancient urban centre with a significant later Buddhist monastic presence.

name: Vadnagar
note: An ancient town with a Buddhist monastic complex, visited by the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang.

name: Devni Mori
note: A Buddhist stupa site in Gujarat that yielded a dated reliquary casket with Buddha relics, an important chronological anchor for the region.

name: Bagh Caves
note: Also covered under Ancient Cave Sites — Buddhist rock-cut caves with murals in a style close to Ajanta's.

name: Sirpur
note: Also covered under Jain sites — an early-historic site with Buddhist, Hindu and Jain remains side by side.

name: Lalitgiri / Ratnagiri / Udayagiri
note: A cluster of three major Buddhist monastic sites in Odisha (distinct from the Jain Udayagiri-Khandagiri caves near Bhubaneswar), sometimes called Odisha's "Diamond Triangle".

name: Ellora Caves
note: Also covered under World Heritage, Cave and Jain sites — includes a distinct group of Buddhist caves alongside its Hindu and Jain ones.

name: Kanheri Caves
note: Also covered under Ancient Cave Sites — one of the largest Buddhist cave complexes in India, in present-day Mumbai.

name: Kanaganahalli
note: A Satavahana-era Buddhist stupa site notable for a rare sculpted relief explicitly labelled as a portrait of Ashoka.

name: Guntupalli Caves
note: Also covered under Ancient Cave Sites — a Buddhist rock-cut monastic complex with a notable circular chaitya hall.

name: Anuradhapura
note: Ancient capital of Sri Lanka and a major early Buddhist centre — home to the Sri Maha Bodhi, said to be grown from a cutting of the original Bodh Gaya tree.

name: Sigiriya
note: A rock fortress and later Buddhist monastic site in Sri Lanka, famed for its frescoes — not part of India, but frequently grouped with the subcontinent's Buddhist heritage sites on reference maps.

name: Martand Sun Temple
note: An 8th-century CE Kashmiri sun temple built under Lalitaditya Muktapida, now in ruins.

name: Masrur Rock-Cut Temple Complex
note: A group of monolithic rock-cut temples, unusual for being carved directly from a hillside rather than built, in a style recalling Ellora.

name: Hidimba Devi Temple
note: A distinctive wooden pagoda-style temple in Manali, an unusual regional architectural form.

name: Khatarmal Sun Temple
note: One of the oldest sun temples in India, in the Kumaon hills near Almora.

name: Da Parbatia Temple Site
note: Yielded the earliest known example of Gupta-style temple door-frame sculpture in Assam, though the main structure hasn't survived.

name: Kamakhya Temple
note: A major Shakti Peetha, one of the most important centres of Tantric worship in India.

name: Sibsagar
note: Former Ahom capital with several major temples (Shivadol, Vishnudol, Devidol) built under Ahom patronage.

name: Pushkar
note: Home to one of the very few temples in India dedicated to Brahma.

name: Nagari (Ancient Madhyamika)
note: Site of ancient Madhyamika, with one of the earliest known Vaishnava temple/pillar remains in India (associated with the Ghosundi/Hathibada inscriptions).

name: Mount Abu
note: Also covered under Jain sites — home to the intricately carved Dilwara Temples.

name: Modhera Sun Temple
note: An 11th-century CE sun temple built under the Solanki (Chalukya) dynasty, with a stepped surya-kund (tank) in front.

name: Deogarh, Dashavatar Temple
note: Also covered under Jain sites — the Dashavatara Temple here is one of the earliest surviving Gupta-era Hindu stone temples, with a landmark Panchayatana layout.

name: Shiv Temple, Bhojpur
note: An unfinished 11th-century Shiva temple built under Raja Bhoja, with one of the largest Shiva lingams in India.

name: Bhitargaon Temple
note: The oldest known surviving brick Hindu temple in India, from the Gupta period.

name: Khajuraho
note: Also covered under World Heritage and Jain sites — Chandela-era temples famous for elaborate sculptural work.

name: Nachna Kuthara, Parvati Temple
note: An early (Gupta-era) stone temple, notable for its preserved original form and sculpture.

name: Tigawa Temple
note: One of the earliest surviving Gupta-era stone temples, an important reference point for the development of Hindu temple architecture.

name: Vishnupur (Bishnupur)
note: Former Malla-dynasty capital known for a distinctive terracotta temple architecture style, mostly from the 17th–18th centuries.

name: Somnath Temple
note: One of the twelve Jyotirlinga shrines, repeatedly destroyed and rebuilt across history — most famously sacked by Mahmud of Ghazni in 1025 CE.

name: Ellora, Kailashnath Temple
note: Also covered under World Heritage, Cave, Jain and Buddhist sites — the Kailasa Temple here is a single monolithic structure carved top-down from one rock, under the Rashtrakutas.

name: Fifteen Temples, Lonar
note: A cluster of medieval temples around the Lonar crater lake, a rare meteor-impact site.

name: Sirpur Temple Complex (Laxman Temple)
note: Also covered under Jain and Buddhist sites — the Laxman Temple here is a notable early brick temple.

name: Bhubaneshwar
note: Home to a dense concentration of Kalinga-style temples, including the Lingaraj Temple, spanning several centuries of temple architecture.

name: Puri
note: Site of the Jagannath Temple, one of the Char Dham (four sacred pilgrimage) sites of Hinduism.

name: Konark (Sun Temple)
note: Also covered under World Heritage sites — built under the Eastern Ganga dynasty in the form of a colossal stone chariot.

name: Aihole
note: Also covered under Jain sites — an early Chalukya temple town, often called a "cradle" of Indian temple architecture for its experimental variety of styles.

name: Pattadakal
note: Also covered under World Heritage and Jain sites — a Chalukya complex deliberately blending Nagara and Dravida styles side by side.

name: Badami
note: Also covered under Cave and Jain sites — Chalukya-dynasty rock-cut temples carved into a sandstone cliff.

name: Hampi
note: Also covered under World Heritage sites — ruins of Vijayanagara, with numerous major temples including the Virupaksha Temple.

name: Halebidu
note: Former Hoysala capital, home to the Hoysaleswara Temple, famed for extraordinarily detailed soapstone carving.

name: Tirupati
note: Site of the Venkateswara Temple, among the most-visited pilgrimage sites in the world.

name: Kanchipuram
note: Also covered under Jain sites — a major temple city under the Pallavas and later the Cholas.

name: Mahabalipuram (Mamallapuram)
note: Also covered under World Heritage, Important Kingdoms & Towns, and Cave sites — Pallava-era rock-cut rathas and the Shore Temple.

name: Gangaikondacholapuram
note: Built by Rajendra I to mark a new Chola capital, its temple is part of the "Great Living Chola Temples" World Heritage listing.

name: Sri Rangnathswamy Temple
note: One of the largest functioning Hindu temple complexes in the world, at Srirangam near Tiruchirapalli.

name: Thanjavur (Brihadeeswara Temple)
note: Also covered under World Heritage sites — built under Raja Raja Chola I, part of the "Great Living Chola Temples" listing.

name: Madurai
note: Site of the Meenakshi Amman Temple, a major centre of Dravidian temple architecture, mainly from the Nayaka period.
